papers.abstract: Motivated by the long-standing ``${\pi}{\pi}$ puzzle'' in nonleptonic $B$ decays, we revisit the $B$ ${\to}$ ${\pi}{\pi}$ decays within the QCD factorization (QCDF) framework, now incorporating the soft color-octet matrix element (COME) contributions, an ingredient that has been largely overlooked in earlier QCDF studies. A comprehensive phenomenological analysis is performed under three distinct scenarios, with the free parameters determined via fits to the available experimental data using the ${\chi}^{2}$ method. The goodness-of-fit is very poor for Scenario S1, which corresponds to the traditional QCDF case without the soft COME contributions, and for Scenario S2, which includes the soft COME contributions but omits the weak annihilation (WA) contributions. Scenario S3, in which both the COME and WA contributions are included simultaneously, achieves an excellent overall fit. In Scenario S3, the QCDF approach can accommodate almost all $B$ ${\to}$ ${\pi}{\pi}$ observables in a consistent and satisfactory manner, and the fitted parameters ${\rho}_{A}$ $<$ $1$ (WA) and ${\rho}_{c}$ ${\sim}$ $0.3$ (soft COME) are in good agreement with the QCDF power counting scheme and the factorization hypothesis.

papers.title: RAG vs. GraphRAG: A Systematic Evaluation and Key Insights
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves large language models (LLMs) by retrieving relevant information from external sources and has been widely adopted for text-based tasks. For structured data, such as knowledge graphs, Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) retrieves and aggregates information along graph structures. More recently, GraphRAG has been extended to general text settings by organizing unstructured text into graph representations, showing promise for reasoning and grounding. Despite these advances, existing GraphRAG systems for text data are often tailored to specific tasks, datasets, and system designs, resulting in heterogeneous evaluation protocols. Consequently, a systematic understanding of the relative strengths, limitations, and trade-offs between RAG and GraphRAG on widely used text benchmarks remains limited. In this paper, we present a comprehensive benchmark study comparing RAG and GraphRAG on established text-based tasks, including question answering and query-based summarization. We introduce a unified evaluation protocol that standardizes data preprocessing, retrieval configurations, and generation settings, enabling fair and reproducible comparisons. Our results highlight the distinct strengths of RAG and GraphRAG across different tasks and evaluation perspectives. Building on these findings, we explore selection and integration strategies that combine the strengths of both paradigms, leading to consistent performance improvements. We further analyze failure modes, efficiency trade-offs, and evaluation biases, and highlight key considerations for designing and evaluating retrieval-augmented generation systems.

papers.title: Language in the Flow of Time: Time-Series-Paired Texts Weaved into a Unified Temporal Narrative
papers.abstract: While many advances in time series models focus exclusively on numerical data, research on multimodal time series, particularly those involving contextual textual information, remains in its infancy. With recent progress in large language models and time series learning, we revisit the integration of paired texts with time series through the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, which posits that representations of different modalities converge to shared spaces. In this context, we identify that time-series-paired texts may naturally exhibit periodic properties that closely mirror those of the original time series. Building on this insight, we propose a novel framework, Texts as Time Series (TaTS), which considers the time-series-paired texts to be auxiliary variables of the time series. TaTS can be plugged into any existing numerical-only time series models and effectively enable them to handle time series data with paired texts. Through extensive experiments on both multimodal time series forecasting and imputation tasks across benchmark datasets with various existing time series models, we demonstrate that TaTS can enhance multimodal predictive performance without modifying model architectures. Our Code is available at https://github.com/iDEA-iSAIL-Lab-UIUC/TaTS.

papers.title: Explanation Design in Strategic Learning: Sufficient Explanations That Induce Non-harmful Responses
papers.abstract: We study the design of explanations in algorithmic decision-making with strategic agents, individuals who may modify their inputs in response to explanations of a decision maker's (DM's) predictive model. While the demand for algorithmic transparency has led much prior work to assume full model disclosure, in practice DMs typically provide only partial information via explanations, which can cause agents to misinterpret the model and take actions that unintentionally reduce their own utility. A central open question is therefore how DMs should communicate explanations that avoid harming strategic agents while still supporting their own goals, e.g., minimising predictive error. In this work, we analyse widely used explanation methods and establish a necessary condition to prevent explanations from inducing self-harming responses. Furthermore, we show that action recommendation-based explanations (ARexes), which encompass counterfactual explanations, are sufficient to induce all non-harmful responses. Under a conditional homogeneity assumption, this sufficiency extends to ARex-generating methods, echoing the revelation principle in information design. To demonstrate their practical utility, we introduce a simple learning procedure that jointly optimises the predictive model and the explanation-generating policy. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world tasks show that ARexes enable DMs to achieve high predictive performance while preserving agents' utility, offering a principled strategy for safe and effective partial model disclosure.

papers.title: Why Transformers Struggle with Distribution-Independent In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: With in-context learning (ICL), transformer models adapt to new tasks from illustrative examples at inference time without updating their parameters. A common interpretation is that transformers implement implicit learning algorithms in their forward pass. We test this interpretation and ICL capability under distribution shift in noiseless polynomial regression, where the context uniquely determines the target function. Models that are near-perfect in distribution exhibit sharp performance degradation under shifts in the input or target-function distribution. This behavior persists across polynomial degrees and multiple training interventions, and in higher-dimensional nonlinear regression. We identify two architectural mechanisms that explain this breakdown: output saturation at finite boundary values linked to final normalization, and attention concentration on a small subset of the context, which can limit context-dependent adaptation required for ICL. Controlled experiments, architectural ablations, targeted interventions, and theoretical analysis provide strong evidence for both mechanisms and their consequence: strong in-distribution ICL does not imply distribution-independent ICL, which calls for caution when using ICL instead of explicit retraining or adaptation under distribution shift.

papers.title: Enforcing Demographic Coherence: A Harms Aware Framework for Reasoning about Private Data Release
papers.abstract: The technical literature about data privacy largely consists of two complementary approaches: formal definitions of conditions sufficient for privacy preservation and attacks that demonstrate privacy breaches. Differential privacy is an accepted standard in the former sphere. However, differential privacy's powerful adversarial model and worst-case guarantees may make it too stringent in some situations, especially when achieving it comes at a significant cost to data utility. Meanwhile, privacy attacks aim to expose real and worrying privacy risks associated with existing data release processes but often face criticism for being unrealistic. Moreover, the literature on attacks generally does not identify what properties are necessary to defend against them. We address the gap between these approaches by introducing demographic coherence, a condition inspired by privacy attacks that we argue is necessary for data privacy. This condition captures privacy violations arising from inferences about individuals that are incoherent with respect to the demographic patterns in the data. Our framework focuses on confidence rated predictors, which can in turn be distilled from almost any data-informed process. Thus, we capture privacy threats that exist even when no attack is explicitly being carried out. Our framework not only provides a condition with respect to which data release algorithms can be analysed but suggests natural experimental evaluation methodologies that could be used to build practical intuition and make tangible assessment of risks. Finally, we argue that demographic coherence is weaker than differential privacy: we prove that every differentially private data release is also demographically coherent, and that there are demographically coherent algorithms which are not differentially private.

papers.title: Finite convergence and minimizer extraction in moment relaxations with correlative sparsity
papers.abstract: We identify a new sufficient condition for the finite convergence of moment relaxations of polynomial optimization problems with correlative sparsity. This condition, which follows from a solution to a correlatively sparse version of the classical truncated moment problem, requires that certain moment matrices admit a flat extension and that the variable cliques underpinning the relaxation satisfy a "running intersection" property. We also describe an algorithm that, when these conditions are met, extracts at least as many minimizers for the original polynomial optimization problem as the largest rank of the moment matrices in its relaxation. Our results, along with the necessity of the running intersection property, are illustrated with examples.

papers.title: Ultrametric approximation and Gromov--Hausdorff clouds
papers.abstract: We compute the Gromov--Hausdorff distance from a metric space to the class of ultrametric spaces in terms of its ultrametric defect and study when a compact ultrametric space attains this distance. For the product of a compact ultrametric space and a compact connected metric space, we give a criterion for the existence of such an approximation. For every integer $k\geqslant1$, we obtain an exact formula for the distance from a bounded metric space to the class of ultrametric spaces with at most $k$ points and prove that the minimum is attained. We characterize the clouds that contain a path-connected space. For compact $X$, we construct a geodesic of length $\operatorname{diam}\textbf{U}(X)/2$ to a nearest connected compact space.

papers.title: Graded String Diagrams with Applications in Probabilistic Reasoning
papers.abstract: We introduce string diagrams for graded symmetric monoidal categories. Our approach includes a definition of graded monoidal theory and the corresponding freely generated syntactic category. The para construction on monoidal actegories is a motivating example for our framework, and we show how an axiomatic presentation of the resulting category $\mathbf{Para}(\mathbb{G},\mathbf{C})$ may be modularly obtained from presentations for $\mathbb{G}$ and $\mathbf{C}$. We demonstrate three different applications of our diagrammatic language under the same theme: probabilistic reasoning. First, we show how to axiomatise a variant of the graded category $\mathbf{ImP}$, recently introduced by Liell-Cock and Staton to model imprecise probability. This culminates in a representation, as string diagrams with grading wires, of programs with primitives for nondeterministic and probabilistic choices and conditioning. Second, we exploit our modular presentation result to provide a new proof for a presentation of $\mathbf{Gauss}$, the category of Gaussian stochastic maps. Third, we use grading wires to represent causal interventions on Bayesian networks.

papers.title: Noncommutative Hourglasses I: On the Classification of Q-Fano 3-Folds of Gorenstein Index 2 via Derived Categories
papers.abstract: In previous work, Takagi used the methods of solving the Sarkisov links by calculating the corresponding Diophantine equations and the construction of key varieties to give all possible classifications and some implementations of a class $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano 3-fold with Fano index 1/2 and at worst $(1, 1, 1)/2$ or QODP singularities. Firstly, we use a method different from Kawamata's work to give the derived category formulas for general weighted blow-up and Kawamata weighted blow-up. On this basis, we study the changing behavior of the derived category of Takagi's varieties under Sarkisov links. Finally, by studying non-commutative projections, we give exceptional collections on the derived category of Takagi's varieties and their corresponding geometric meanings.

papers.title: Simulation of Micro-Void Development within Large Scale Additively Manufactured Polymer Composite Deposition Beads
papers.abstract: Despite the growing level of technology advancement that characterizes extrusion deposition additive manufacturing technology, there remains significant knowledge gap in fully understanding the process-structure-property relationship involved in this technology. The ability to effectively and efficiently control the manufacturing process provides an opportunity for optimizing the complex microstructure of the polymer composite prints which can lead to significant improvement of the associated print properties and in-service part performance. Modeling the polymer melt flow extrusion-deposition process is important in understanding the development of the inherent microstructural formation. The current research presents a computational-based approach for investigating process induced micro-voids and their impact on print properties. We develop a multiscale FEA simulation tool to predict the global and local flow-fields during the polymer-melt flow process to investigate underlying mechanisms that may promote the micro-void development within the bead microstructure and determine potential process related factors that can be controlled to mitigate micro-void formation and growth. The research also presents a computational based method for assessing the impact of the micro-voids on the effective print properties. The direct implication of a reduced part voidage levels is the development of high-quality functional components for specialized applications such as light weight & high strength integrity composites widely used in a variety of industries particularly the automobile, aerospace, renewable energy and defense industries.

papers.title: Quantifier Elimination and Craig Interpolation, Quantitatively
papers.abstract: Quantifier elimination (QE) and Craig interpolation (CI) are central to various state-of-the-art automated approaches to hardware- and software verification. They are rooted in the Boolean setting and are successful for, e.g., first-order theories such as linear rational arithmetic. What about their applicability in the quantitative setting where formulae evaluate to numbers and quantitative supremum/infimum quantifiers are the natural counterpart to Boolean quantifiers? Applications include establishing quantitative properties of programs such as bounds on expected outcomes of probabilistic programs featuring non-determinism and analyzing the flow of information through programs. In this paper, we present, to the best of our knowledge, the first QE algorithm for possibly unbounded, $\infty$- or $(-\infty)$-valued, or discontinuous piecewise linear quantities. They are the quantitative counterpart to linear rational arithmetic, and they are a popular quantitative assertion language for probabilistic program verification. We provide rigorous soundness proofs as well as upper bounds on the size of the output. Moreover, we present two applications of our QE algorithm. First, our algorithm yields a quantitative CI theorem: Given arbitrary piecewise linear quantities $f,g$ with $f \models g$ (i.e., $f$ is at most $g$ at every variable valuation), both the strongest and the weakest Craig interpolants are quantifier-free and effectively constructible. Such interpolants lie between the two quantities and use only their common free variables. Second, we apply our QE algorithm to computing minimal and maximal expected outcomes of loop-free probabilistic programs featuring unbounded non-determinism, and to checking inductivity of candidate upper bounds on minimal and maximal expected outcomes of probabilistic loops featuring unbounded non-determinism.

papers.title: The Maximum Number of Sets for 12 Cards is 14
papers.abstract: We analyze a mathematical property of the popular card game SET. We present a revised geometric and computer-assisted proof that the maximum number of sets for 12 cards is 14 using finite field geometry, combinatorics, and graph theory. We present several computer algorithms for finding or approximating the maximum number of sets. We show a complete computer proof that iterates over all possible board configurations. We use this method to compute the maximum number of sets with 4 properties for a small number of cards, but it is generally too inefficient. With this method, we compute the maximum number of sets for 3 properties for all possible numbers of cards. Finally, we compare this to an existing approximation algorithm for finding maximal sets.

papers.title: Smoothed Analysis of Nash Equilibrium and Fixed Point Computation, and Efficiency of the Homotopy Method
papers.abstract: We study, under a smoothed analysis perspective, the complexity of three PPAD-complete problems: computing Nash equilibria, computing fixed points, and solving variational inequalities. We consider a general perturbation model that bounds the probability density of the quantities evaluated by our algorithms. As special cases, it captures worst-case games perturbed by small random per-action costs, and worst-case maps perturbed by a small random affine function. Under these models, we show that classical algorithmic paradigms, cover-based search and homotopy path-following provably outperform the worst-case state-of-the-art. For games with a constant number of players and $n$ strategies per player, a recursive cover-based algorithm computes an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium using $\log(1/\varepsilon)\cdot 2^{O(n)}$ expected payoff-vector computations, compared to the worst-case runtime tradeoffs of $\log(1/\varepsilon)\cdot n^{O(n)}$, $(1/\varepsilon)^{O(n)}$, $2^{O(\log^2 n/\varepsilon^2)}$, and $2^{O(n)}\mathrm{poly}(\log(1/\varepsilon))$. For fixed points and variational inequalities of bounded and Lipschitz maps on the $n$-dimensional $\ell_2$ unit ball, the same approach runs in expected time $\log(1/\varepsilon)\cdot 2^{O(n)}$, compared to the worst-case $(1/\varepsilon)^{O(n)}$; the $2^{\Omega(n)}$ factor is necessary by prior work [Rubinstein, 2017]. For general smooth maps, we further analyze the classical predictor--corrector homotopy method, for which only qualitative convergence guarantees were previously known, showing that under perturbations the homotopy path is well conditioned and has length $2^{O(n)}$, so that the method finds an $\varepsilon$-approximate solution in time $2^{O(n)}\cdot\mathrm{poly}(1/p)/\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-p$.

papers.title: High-quality electron beam generation from laser wakefield accelerators for driving compact free electron lasers
papers.abstract: Despite the successful demonstration of compact free electron lasers (FELs) driven by laser wakefield accelerators (LWFAs), the pursuit of further enhancements in high-gain compact FELs presents a challenge due to the limitations in electron beam quality. In this work, we pinpoint the pivotal physics and optimization strategies for high-quality single-stage LWFAs that are crucial for high-gain FELs. We have delved into the synergistic injection mechanism, where the self-evolution injection threshold is far from reached at the injection position, with both the shock front and self-evolution of the laser playing a role in the injection process. A thorough discussion has been provided on the beam-quality degradation and optimization strategies, in terms of global (slice) energy spread and projected (slice) emittance. With the goal of achieving high-gain FELs driven by LWFAs, we have also explored the synthesis quality of the electron beam to determine an optimized power gain length. A comprehensive start-to-end simulation has been conducted, demonstrating the effectiveness of compact FELs powered by these high-quality electron beams. The resulting radiation reaches the saturation regime after a 4.5-meter-long undulator, with an energy of 17.4 {\mu}J and a power of 6.0 GW at a wavelength of 23.9 nm. This proposed scheme offers not only a framework for optimizing beam quality in LWFAs, but also a promising path for future compact LWFA-driven FELs to achieve saturated regimes, opening up new possibilities for widespread applications.

papers.title: Viral Lattice Theory: A Biophysical Framework for Collective Virion Motion
papers.abstract: Viral Lattice Theory develops a testable framework for collective motion and mechanical response of virions and virus-like particles (VLPs) in viscoelastic environments. Its central problem is observational ambiguity: distinct interparticle forces, material relaxation processes, and hydrodynamic couplings can produce similar particle trajectories or equilibrium measurements. We ask which additional measurements can distinguish these mechanisms. Combining lattice dynamics, stochastic mechanics, and linear response theory, the framework derives memory-dependent forces and, under thermal-equilibrium assumptions, fluctuation-dissipation-consistent noise. Explicit observation models account for finite camera exposure and support parameter-identifiability tests and experimental design. In a synthetic response-fluctuation benchmark, models with matching equilibrium covariance and nearly matching response magnitude differ by approximately 28 degrees in response phase and 40% in spectral density at a selected crossover, demonstrating the discriminating value of complementary observables. A crystal-response example uses satellite tobacco mosaic virus geometry and published acoustic summaries to calibrate a spectral peak and test a separately reserved linewidth. An HPV-inspired VLP model extends the framework to classical stochastic transport between intact, reversibly deformed, and damaged structural states, illustrating recovery and delayed damage after delivery. Path-survival and driven-cycle calculations distinguish transient loading from sustained nonequilibrium behavior. A separate viral-phonon quantization postulate is presented as a conditional quantum extension, not an established biological effect. The results provide synthetic and conditional comparisons that specify experimentally testable distinctions.

papers.title: Torsion of elliptic curves over quartic number fields with rational $j$-invariant
papers.abstract: Let $E$ be an elliptic curve defined over a quartic extension $K$ of $\mathbb{Q}$ with $j(E)\in\mathbb{Q}$. We classify the possible group structures of $E(K)_{\mathrm{tors}}$, concluding that the only additional possibilities, besides those occuring over quartic fields by base change from elliptic curves over $\mathbb{Q}$, are $\mathbb{Z}/17\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}/21\mathbb{Z}$.

papers.title: High-Dimensional Markov-Switching Ordinary Differential Processes
papers.abstract: Complex systems often evolve in continuous time but are observed only at discrete time points with measurement noise. When the interactions can change across unobserved states, recovering both the state transitions and the differential equations is important for mechanistic insight and for identifying time-varying directed graphs. However, this recovery is challenging in high dimensions. In this paper, we study estimation and graph recovery for high-dimensional Markov-switching ordinary differential equation models from noisy discrete observations. We model the switching between states by a latent continuous-time Markov chain, and within each state the drift is a sparse additive function with unknown nonlinear components. We approximate each component by a finite basis expansion and estimate the parameters under group sparsity. Our procedure estimates the latent trajectories by wavelet smoothing and then runs a penalized surrogate expectation-maximization algorithm. Under stationarity and geometric $\beta$-mixing, given a sufficiently accurate estimated trajectory and other local regularity conditions, we show that the algorithm converges geometrically to a neighborhood of the true parameters. Finally, in an application to resting-state fMRI data, the procedure identifies multiple connectivity states, whose occupation times we compare descriptively between the children with combined-type ADHD and the typically developing children used in the fit.

papers.title: Paleoinspired Vision: From Exploring Colour Vision Evolution to Inspiring Camera Design
papers.abstract: The evolution of colour vision is captivating, as it reveals the adaptive strategies of extinct species while simultaneously inspiring innovations in modern imaging technology. In this study, we present a simplified model of visual transduction in the retina, introducing a novel opsin layer. We quantify evolutionary pressures by measuring machine vision recognition accuracy on colour images shaped by specific opsins. Building on this, we develop an evolutionary conservation optimisation algorithm to reconstruct the spectral sensitivity of opsins, enabling mutation-driven adaptations to more effectively spot fruits or predators. This model condenses millions of years of evolution into seconds using GPU, providing an experimental framework to test long-standing hypotheses in evolutionary biology, such as vision of early mammals, primate trichromacy from gene duplication, retention of colour blindness, blue-shift of fish rod and multiple rod opsins with bioluminescence. Beyond validating existing paleontological hypotheses, our model further enables speculative explorations of hypothetical species, such as organisms with visual systems adapted to Martian conditions. These constitute our contributions to AI for life science and neuroscience. Besides, the principles derived from these biological studies can translate into practical engineering solutions. In practice, our findings suggest a minimalist yet effective approach to task-specific camera filter design, optimising the spectral response function to meet application-driven demands. Code repository: https://github.com/luyijie-research/PaleVision.

papers.title: Accelerating AIGC Services with Latent Action Diffusion Scheduling in Edge Networks
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) has gained significant popularity for creating diverse content. However, current AIGC models primarily focus on content quality within a centralized framework, resulting in a high service delay and negative user experiences. The workload of an AIGC task is determined by model complexity and multi-layered encoder architectures, posing significant challenges for its modeling, deployment, and scheduling within resource-constrained edge networks. We model an offloading problem among edges for providing real AIGC services and propose \textbf{LAD-TS}, a novel Latent Action Diffusion-based Task Scheduling method that orchestrates multiple edge servers for expedited AIGC services by leveraging the diffusion model's conditional guidance capability and the reinforcement learning's environment interaction ability. We first design an innovative Latent Action Diffusion Network (LADN) model based on traditional diffusion models. We then incorporate the LADN model into deep reinforcement learning, forming an effective LAD-TS method for task scheduling in distributed edge networks. Meanwhile, we design a latent action diffusion strategy to achieve near-optimal decisions quickly by utilizing historical action probabilities instead of Gaussian noise. Furthermore, we implement a refined AIGC model and develop \textbf{DEdgeAI}, a prototype edge system with the refined AIGC model deployment to evaluate our LAD-TS method. DEdgeAI provides a real AIGC service for users, demonstrating up to $7.36\%-18.11\%$ and $34.07\%-94.96\%$ shorter service delays than the state-of-the-art methods and representative commercial platforms, respectively. We release our open-source code at https://github.com/ChangfuXu/DEdgeAI/

papers.title: EcoSearch: A Constant-Delay Best-First Search Algorithm for Program Synthesis
papers.abstract: Many approaches to program synthesis perform a combinatorial search within a large space of programs to find one that satisfies a given specification. To tame the search space blowup, previous works introduced probabilistic and neural approaches to guide this combinatorial search by inducing heuristic cost functions. Best-first search algorithms ensure to search in the exact order induced by the cost function, significantly reducing the portion of the program space to be explored. A key limitation of existing best-first search algorithms is that they slow down over time: the delay between outputting successive programs grows with the number of programs already generated. We ask whether best-first search algorithms with constant delay exist. We design Eco Search, a new best-first bottom-up search algorithm. It combines the cost tuple representation of Bee Search with the per non-terminal data structures of Heap Search, thanks to a new frugal expansion strategy, and it uses bucket queues instead of priority queues, which is possible because the costs stored in each queue always lie in a window of constant width. We prove that Eco Search is the first constant-delay best-first search algorithm for pre-generation cost functions. Experimentally, we evaluate Eco Search on two classic program-synthesis benchmarks (DeepCoder and FlashFill) and observe that Eco Search solves 12% to 70% more tasks than its predecessors, and reaches the number of tasks they solve 1.6 to 3.2 times faster. This shows that constant delay can be achieved for best-first search in program synthesis, and that it makes a difference in practice.

papers.title: ViDE: Tuning-Free Video Coherence via Temporal Attention Reweighting and Prompt Blending
papers.abstract: Despite the substantial progress in long video generation, multi-prompt synthesis often encounters inconsistencies resulting from the training-inference gap caused by length extension techniques and coarse prompt interpolation. To overcome these issues, we propose the Video Diffusion with hidden states Editing (ViDE) framework, which consists of two key components. The first is the Time-frequency based Temporal Attention Reweighting (TiTAR) algorithm, which leverages the relationship between inconsistencies and diagonal elements of temporal attention. By reweighting the attention scores via the Discrete Short-Time Fourier Transform (DSTFT), TiTAR effectively reduces frame inconsistencies, a capability further corroborated by a Fourier-based analysis. The second component, PromptBlend, reduces inconsistencies in multi-prompt settings through fine-grained prompt alignment and adaptive interpolation, enabling smooth semantic transitions. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of ViDE, demonstrating consistent and significant improvements over multiple baselines.

papers.title: Embedded Decomposed Transformer for explainable multivariate time series forecasting
papers.abstract: Time series forecasting is an important problem with diverse real-world applications. This paper introduces the Embedded Decomposed Transformer (EDformer) for multivariate time series forecasting. EDformer decomposes the input signal into seasonal and trend components using two complementary strategies: time-domain Average Pooling (AP) based on moving-average smoothing and Frequency-Aware (FA) decomposition based on low-pass filtering in the Fourier domain. The reconstructed multivariate seasonal component is embedded across inverted dimensions, after which attention captures cross-variate correlations and a feed-forward network learns nonlinear representations for each variable. The trend component is forecast through projection and combined with the seasonal prediction to produce the final forecast. We evaluate both decomposition variants on several real-world datasets, showing that EDformer achieves competitive performance, while their relative effectiveness varies across datasets, experimental settings, and temporal characteristics. We further conduct an ablation study isolating the contribution of decomposition, inverted embedding, and the frequency cutoff ratio; a hyperparameter sensitivity analysis over learning rate and batch size; and a statistical significance analysis using Friedman and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests to substantiate the reported performance differences. Finally, model explainability techniques are explored to improve interpretability and provide insights into the features and time steps influencing the forecasting results.

papers.title: Non-collapsed RCD spaces with local bounded covering geometry
papers.abstract: We study non-collapsed $\mathrm{RCD}(-(N-1),N)$ spaces with locally bounded covering geometry. Our first main result generalizes Gromov's almost flat manifold theorem: if the universal cover is non-collapsing and the diameter is sufficiently small, then the space is bi-Holder homeomorphic to an infranilmanifold. In the smooth setting with $\mathrm{Ric} \ge -(N-1)$, this homeomorphism is actually a diffeomorphism. As an application of our arguments, we show that Gromov's almost flat manifold theorem extends to the $\mathrm{RCD}+\mathrm{CBA}$ setting. Our second main result generalizes Fukaya's fibration theorem. Suppose a sequence of non-collapsed $\mathrm{RCD}(-(N-1),N)$ spaces with locally bounded covering geometry converges in the pointed measured Gromov--Hausdorff sense to a smooth manifold of dimension $k < N$. We then construct a topological fiber bundle map from the RCD spaces to the limit manifold. The fibers are infranilmanifolds, and the structure group is affine. Finally, although there exist collapsing Ricci limit spaces with no topological manifold points, we prove that if the sequence additionally satisfies locally bounded covering geometry and the limit space has dimension $k$, then every $k$-regular point is a topological manifold point.

papers.title: Self-correcting qubit in a strongly driven LC resonator
papers.abstract: We propose a device to realize quantum error correction by dissipation. The device generates Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states as steady states in a single driven LC resonator. The resonator should have impedance above $h/2e^2\approx 12.9\,{\rm k}\Omega$, and should be driven across a Josephson junction with a high-amplitude voltage tone at frequency near-commensurate with the resonator frequency. In this regime, we show that GKP states emerge as steady-states of the resonator; these states encode a qubit protected against phase-space local noise. Low-lying excitations preserve the quantum information and increase the energy proportionally to a measure of the error degree. Thus, quantum error correction of both bit and phase errors can be achieved with dissipative cooling. Our calculations indicate an achievable coherence time of $ 1000 \times$ the resonator photon lifetime at operating temperatures above $100 \, {\rm mK}$. Beyond steady-state quantum error correction, the device supports protected single-qubit Clifford gates and readout with exponential accuracy corrected by the same dissipative mechanism, as well as magic-state preparation above the distillation threshold.

papers.title: Human-Machine Interfaces for Subsea Telerobotics: From Soda-straw to Natural Language Interactions
papers.abstract: This review explores the evolution of human-machine interfaces (HMIs) in subsea telerobotics, charting the progression from traditional first-person "soda-straw" consoles-- characterized by narrow field-of-view camera feeds-- to contemporary interfaces leveraging gesture recognition, virtual reality, and natural language processing. The review makes three key contributions. First, we introduce a structured framework that analyzes subsea HMIs through three interrelated aspects: operator experience, robotic autonomy, and bidirectional human-machine communication. Second, using these aspects, we compare visual, haptic, extended-reality, gesture, and natural-language interfaces; examine the progression from direct teleoperation to shared autonomy; and assess the distinct roles of simulators and digital twins in training, prototyping, and mission support. Third, we synthesize the reported evidence to distinguish established industrial tools, selectively deployed technologies, and research-stage capabilities, while identifying limitations in interoperability, communication reliability, immersive feedback, and field validation. From this synthesis, we outline standardization needs and research directions for hydrodynamic feedback, latency-aware shared autonomy, grounded language interaction, and real-to-simulation transfer. The report concludes by identifying open research questions and proposing a roadmap toward more intelligent and intuitive subsea HMI systems.

papers.title: Multi-Label Contrastive Learning : A Comprehensive Study
papers.abstract: Multi-label classification, which involves assigning multiple labels to a single input, has emerged as a key area in both research and industry due to its wide-ranging applications. Designing effective loss functions is crucial for optimizing deep neural networks for this task, as they significantly influence model performance and efficiency. Traditional loss functions, which often maximize likelihood under the assumption of label independence, may struggle to capture complex label relationships. Recent research has turned to supervised contrastive learning, a method that aims to create a structured representation space by bringing similar instances closer together and pushing dissimilar ones apart. Although contrastive learning offers a promising approach, applying it to multi-label classification presents unique challenges, particularly in managing label interactions and data structure. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth study of contrastive learning loss for multi-label classification across diverse settings. These include datasets with both small and large numbers of labels, datasets with varying amounts of training data, and applications in both computer vision and natural language processing. Our empirical results indicate that the promising outcomes of contrastive learning are attributable not only to the consideration of label interactions but also to the robust optimization scheme of the contrastive loss. Furthermore, while the supervised contrastive loss function faces challenges with datasets containing a small number of labels and ranking-based metrics, it demonstrates excellent performance, particularly in terms of Macro-F1, on datasets with a large number of labels.

papers.title: Neural Window Decoding of Spatially Coupled LDPC Codes: Exploiting Window Structure for Learning and Adaptation
papers.abstract: We propose a neural window decoder (NWD) for spatially coupled low-density parity-check (SC-LDPC) codes. The proposed methods adapt neural min-sum decoding to the structure and sequential operation of window decoding. First, target-oriented training restricts the loss to the variable nodes whose decisions are required at each window stage. Second, learned damping factors identify check-node updates that can reuse messages from the preceding iteration. Finally, adaptive weight switching selects weights trained for unreliable inherited information when a previous-window failure is detected. For a length-$20{,}000$ $(3,6)$-regular SC-LDPC code, the target-oriented NWD achieves performance comparable to sum-product window decoding while using min-sum updates. On the reduced target graph, scheduling based on regularized damping factors yields an estimated computational cost 48\% lower than that of full-graph weighted min-sum decoding, while maintaining comparable decoding performance. Adaptive weight switching improves decoding performance by 35\% at 3.0 dB relative to plain weights. These learning methods exploit the properties of window decoding to improve the reliability and computational efficiency of SC-LDPC convolutional codes.

papers.title: Semi-analytical model for the calculation of solar radiation pressure and its effects on a LEO satellite with predicting the change in position vectors using machine learning techniques
papers.abstract: The rapid increase in the deployment of Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites, catering to diverse applications such as communication, Earth observation, environmental monitoring, and scientific research, has significantly amplified the complexity of trajectory management. The current work focuses on calculating and analyzing perturbation effects on a satellite's anticipated trajectory in LEO, considering Solar Radiation Pressure (SRP) as the main perturbing force. The acceleration due to SRP and it's effects on the satellite was calculated using a custom-built Python module mainly based on the hypothesis of the cannonball model. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed model through comprehensive simulations and comparisons with existing analytical and numerical methods. Here, the primary Keplerian orbital characteristics were employed to analyze a simulated low-earth orbit LEO satellite, initially visualizing the satellite's trajectory and ground tracks at a designated altitude. The study also focuses on a comparative analysis of ground stations, primarily considering the main regions of the subcontinent, with revisit time as the key parameter for comparison. In the end, we combine analytical techniques with Machine Learning (ML) algorithms to predict changes in the position vectors of the satellite. Using ML techniques, the model can adaptively learn and refine predictions based on historical data and real-time input, thus improving accuracy over time. In addition, the incorporation of analytical methods allows for a deeper understanding of the underlying physics governing satellite motion, enabling more precise adjustments and corrections.

papers.title: U-WNO:U-Net-enhanced Wavelet Neural Operator for fetal head segmentation
papers.abstract: This article describes the development of a novel U-Net-enhanced Wavelet Neural Operator (U-WNO),which combines wavelet decomposition, operator learning, and an encoder-decoder mechanism. This approach harnesses the superiority of the wavelets in time frequency localization of the functions, and the combine down-sampling and up-sampling operations to generate the segmentation map to enable accurate tracking of patterns in spatial domain and effective learning of the functional mappings to perform regional segmentation. By bridging the gap between theoretical advancements and practical applications, the U-WNO holds potential for significant impact in multiple science and industrial fields, facilitating more accurate decision-making and improved operational efficiencies. The operator is demonstrated for different pregnancy trimesters, utilizing two-dimensional ultrasound images.

papers.title: Deriving Tsallis entropy from $q$-deformed Hamiltonian within a statistical mechanics framework
papers.abstract: The Tsallis entropy, which possesses $q$-additive property, is derived from the first principle employing the non-additive Hamiltonian or the $q$-deformed Hamiltonian with the canonical ensemble assumption in statistical mechanics. Here, the $q$-algebra and properties of $q$-deformed functions are extensively used throughout the derivation. Consequently, the thermodynamic quantities, e.g. internal energy and Helmholtz free energy, are derived and they inherently exhibit the $q$-additivity. From this intriguing connection between Tsallis entropy and the $q$-deformed Hamiltonian, the parameter $q$ encapsulates the intrinsic degree of $q$-additivity for the thermodynamic systems.

papers.title: Rigidity of Five-dimensional Shrinking Gradient Ricci Solitons with Constant Scalar Curvature I
papers.abstract: We investigate five-dimensional shrinking gradient Ricci solion $(M^5, g,f)$ satisfying $Ric+\nabla^2f= \frac{1}{2} g$ with constant scalar curvature. Fern\'{a}ndez-L\'{o}pez and Garc\'\i a-R\'\i o \cite{FR16} proved that the possible values of scalar curvature are $\{0,1,\frac{3}{2}, 2, \frac{5}{2}\}$. If $R=0$, the soliton is isometric to $\mathbb{R}^5$; if $R=2$, the soliton is a finite quotient of ${N}^{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ \cite{FR16}, where ${N}^4$ is a four-dimensional Einstein manifold; if $R=\frac{5}{2}$, the soliton is Einstein \cite{Petersen-Wylie2}. The most difficult cases are $R=\frac{3}{2}$ or $R=1$. In \cite{Li-Ou-Qu-Wu} we proved that it is a finite quotient of $\mathbb{R}^3\times \mathbb{S}^2$ if $R=1$. In this paper, we prove that five-dimensional shrinking gradient Ricci soliton with $R=\frac{3}{2}$ is isometric to a finite quotient of $\mathbb{R}^2\times \mathbb{S}^3$.

papers.title: Simulation Studies For Goodness-of-Fit and Two-Sample Methods For Univariate Data
papers.abstract: We present the results of a large number of simulation studies regarding the power of various goodness-of-fit as well as nonparametric two-sample tests for univariate data. This includes both continuous and discrete data. In general no single method can be relied upon to provide good power, any one method may be quite good for some combination of null hypothesis and alternative and may fail badly for another. Based on the results of these studies we propose a fairly small number of methods chosen such that for any of the case studies included here at least one of the methods has good power. The studies were carried out using the R packages R2sample and Rgof, available from CRAN.

papers.title: Information Aggregation in Markets with Analysts, Experts, and Chatbots
papers.abstract: We study information aggregation when traders interpret public news, such as analyst reports, differently. This differential interpretation injects noise into equilibrium prices, compounding the informational bottleneck caused by noise traders. Next to analysts and experts, we consider the role of ``AI" chatbots, which (i) provide free financial advice and (ii) analyze traders' queries to learn about the asset's fundamental. Our model predicts that (i) chatbots aggregate information more efficiently than markets, (ii) increase trade volume, and (iii) enhance the informational content of prices. Ultimately, the AI platform extracts an absolute informational advantage over other market participants, highlighting a structural shift from information aggregation through market prices to ``AI" platforms.

papers.title: Very fast Bayesian Additive Regression Trees on GPU
papers.abstract: Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) is a nonparametric Bayesian regression technique based on an ensemble of decision trees. It is part of the toolbox of many statisticians. The overall statistical quality of the regression is typically higher than other generic alternatives, and it requires less manual tuning, making it a good default choice. However, it is a niche method compared to natural competitors such as XGBoost, due to the longer running time, making sample sizes above 10000-100000 a nuisance. We present a GPU implementation of BART, up to 500x faster than the previous state of the art, making BART fast enough to be a viable option on large datasets, and showing that BART parallelizes better than its non-Bayesian counterparts. We also find that, to be as practical as tree boosting on large datasets, BART would need a scalable way to infer the number of trees, which we do not provide. Our implementation is available in the Python package bartz.

papers.title: Spectral Limits of the Neumann-Poincar\'e Operator on Degenerating Tori
papers.abstract: We determine the limit of the spectrum of the Neumann-Poincar\'e operator on circular tori as the torus degenerates. As the central hole closes, the spectrum converges to $[-1/2,0]$ together with a set of positive points, which we characterize as eigenvalues of explicit limiting operators. As the cross-section shrinks, the spectrum converges to $[0,1/2]$.

papers.title: Polynomial mixing for the white-forced Navier-Stokes system in the whole space
papers.abstract: We study the mixing properties of the white-forced Navier-Stokes system in the whole space $\mathbb{R}^2$. Assuming that the noise is sufficiently non-degenerate, we prove the uniqueness of stationary measure and polynomial mixing in the dual-Lipschitz metric. The proof combines the coupling method with a Foia\c{s}-Prodi type estimate, weighted growth estimates for trajectories, and an estimate for the Leray projector involving Muckenhoupt $A_2$-class weights.

papers.title: Geometry of multidimensional Farey summation algorithm and frieze patterns
papers.abstract: In this paper we develop a new geometric approach to subtractive continued fraction algorithms in high dimensions. We adapt a version of Farey summation to the geometric techniques proposed by F. Klein in 1895. More specifically we introduce Farey polyhedra and their sails that generalise respectively Klein polyhedra and their sails, and show similar duality properties of the Farey sail integer invariants. The construction of Farey sails is based on the multidimensional generalisation of the Farey tessellation provided by a modification of the continued fraction algorithm introduced by R. W. J. Meester. We classify Farey polyhedra in the combinatorial terms of prismatic diagrams. Prismatic diagrams extend boat polygons introduced by S. Morier-Genoud and V. Ovsienko in the two-dimensional case. As one of the applications of the new theory we get a multidimensional version of Conway-Coxeter frieze patterns. We show that multidimensional frieze patterns satisfy generalised Ptolemy relations.

papers.title: $(t,q)$-Series Invariants of Seifert Manifolds
papers.abstract: Gukov, Pei, Putrov, and Vafa developed a $q$-series invariant of negative definite plumbed $3$-manifolds with spin$^{c}$ structures, building on earlier work of Lawrence and Zagier. This was recently generalized to an an infinite family of two-variable $(t,q)$-series invariants by Akhmechet, Johnson, and Krushkal (AJK). We calculate one such series for all Seifert manifolds with $b_{1}=0.$ These results extend a previous theorem of Liles and McSpirit to any number of exceptional fibers and the Reduction Theorem of Gukov, Svoboda, and Katzarkov to the two-variable case. As a consequence, a previous result of Liles and McSpirit on modularity properties and radial limits is enhanced to a larger family of manifolds. We also calculate the infinite collection of $(t,q)$-series invariants for three infinite families of manifolds, finding mixed modularity properties for one such family.

papers.title: Exploring tidal dissipation in rubble pile binary secondaries using a discrete element model
papers.abstract: In this work, models of rubble pile binary secondaries are simulated in various spin states in a system similar in size and scale to Didymos-Dimorphos. The numerical modeling is performed in the N-body Chrono-based software GRAINS, which simulates gravity, contact, and friction forces acting on non-spherical mass elements. In a high-fidelity, high-performance computational setting, tidal dissipation successfully emerges in the simulations as a consequence of the effects of inter-element contact and friction across thousands of simulated nonspherical mass elements. We devise computational techniques and rigorous numerical procedures for studying tides in the well-established framework of GRAINS. The simulations reveal tidal deformation, phase lag, and secular spin-down, including the transition from super-synchronous rotation to synchronous libration. We also observe the exchange of energy and angular momentum between the secondary's rotation and orbit, and identify the semidiurnal tidal response through spectral and topographical analyses. Using both energy and torque-based calculations, we compute values of $Q/k_{2} \sim O(10^{2})$, whereas this value has been predicted by other studies to lie in the range $10^{2}<Q/k_{2}<10^{6}$. Further study is required to determine whether this result is representative of truly enhanced dissipativity, or a consequence of material or modeling assumptions. More broadly, this framework provides a numerical laboratory for investigating the granular mechanisms underlying tidal dissipation and their relationship to the macroscopic tidal response of rubble-pile bodies.

papers.title: Graph Fourier Neural Kernels: Learning Full PDE Trajectories Across Geometries and Anisotropic Parameter Fields
papers.abstract: High-fidelity simulations of time-dependent nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) are expensive to repeat across families of domains and parameter fields, a cost that recurs in design optimization, uncertainty quantification, and computational medicine. Most neural-operator surrogates require each domain to be mapped onto a common grid or reference shape, and few predict the full time course. We introduce Graph Fourier Neural Kernels (G-FuNK), a neural operator for second-order semilinear PDEs with a diffusive principal part that transfers across geometries and anisotropic diffusion tensors without coordinate maps or diffeomorphisms. A weighted graph and its Laplacian supply a spectral basis that encodes geometry and anisotropy. Shared layers act in this basis, at a cost linear in mesh size after one partial eigendecomposition per geometry, and a neural ODE integrator propagates the learned generator to full spatiotemporal trajectories on unseen domains. Across anisotropic heat flow, stiff reaction-diffusion, FitzHugh-Nagumo, and patient-specific left-atrial electrophysiology on CT-derived surfaces, G-FuNK reproduces held-out trajectories with relative $L^2$ error between 0.046 and 0.160. Its accuracy is comparable to that of a geometry-aware Fourier neural operator on regular domains, and its predictions are unchanged when a rectangular domain is rotated. On left atria, whose venous and valvular openings prevent mapping onto a reference shape, it predicts an 85-ms trajectory in under half a second, against about 5 minutes for finite elements, with a mean activation-time error of 1.73 ms. Accuracy depends on graph construction and is highest when the learned generator is integrated at its training time step.

papers.title: Lazy Qubit Reordering for Accelerating Parallel State-Vector-based Quantum Circuit Simulation
papers.abstract: This article proposes two quantum operation scheduling methods for accelerating parallel state-vector-based quantum circuit simulation using multiple graphics processing units (GPUs). The proposed methods reduce all-to-all communication caused by qubit reordering, which can dominate the overhead of parallel simulation. Our out-of-order approach eliminates redundant reorderings by introducing intentional delays in reordering communications such that multiple reorderings can be aggregated into a single reordering. The delays are carefully introduced based on the principles of time-space tiling, or a cache optimization technique for classical computers, which we use to arrange the execution order of quantum operations. Moreover, we develop these methods tailored for two primary procedures in variational quantum eigensolver simulation: quantum state update (QSU) and expectation value computation (EVC). Our QSU simulation takes an advantage of the hierarchical interconnection of GPU systems to avoid slow inter-node communication. On the other hand, our EVC simulation reduces the number of reorderings by diagonalization of Pauli strings. Experimental validation on 32-GPU executions demonstrates acceleration in QSU and EVC$\unicode{x2014}$up to 54$\times$ and 1,657$\times$, respectively$\unicode{x2014}$compared to an inorder-based method. We believe that our out-of-order approach is useful for accelerating large-scale quantum circuit simulations, including QSU and/or EVC that operate qubits in a regular manner.

papers.title: On the Stokes conjecture for compressible gravity waves of extreme form
papers.abstract: In 1880, G. G. Stokes [Mathematical and Physical Papers, Vol.I] examined an extreme two-dimensional irrotational periodic traveling water wave under the influence of gravity and conjectured a symmetric corner of \(120^\circ\) at the crest. The conjecture was first proved rigorously by Amick, Fraenkel, and Toland [Acta Math. 148 (1982)] and, independently, by Plotnikov [Dinamika Sploshn. Sredy 57 (1982)] via the Nekrasov integral equation. In the early 2010s, Varvarua and Weiss [Acta Math. 206 (2011)] revisited the conjecture by introducing a novel geometric method, which provided an affirmative answer to the conjecture without requiring the structural assumptions used in earlier works, such as the isolation of the stagnation points and the symmetry and monotonicity of the free surface. The main purpose of this paper is to establish the validity of the Stokes conjecture in the context of compressible gravity water waves. More precisely, we prove that, at each stagnation point of a compressible gravity water wave, a sharp crest with an included angle of \(120^\circ\) forms, which gives the first rigorous confirmation of the compressible counterpart of the classical Stokes conjecture of 1880. The central aspect of our approach is the discovery of a new monotonicity formula and a modified version of it for quasilinear free boundary problems of Bernoulli type. Another key ingredient is a new nonlinear frequency formula, which we combine with the concentration-cancellation theory of Evans and Muller [J. Amer. Math. Soc. 7 (1994)]. These newly developed monotonicity formulas are valid for nonlinear problems and enable us to carry out a blow-up analysis at each stagnation point and to provide a complete classification of the blow-up limits near each stagnation point.

papers.title: Generative AI, Managerial Expectations, and Economic Activity
papers.abstract: Using generative AI, we extract managers' economic expectations from over 120,000 corporate conference call transcripts. The resulting AI Economy Score predicts GDP growth, production, employment, and wages five or more quarters ahead, beyond survey forecasts and other existing measures. Industry- and firm-level scores capture sector- and firm-specific activity, and a composite of firm, industry, and macroeconomic expectations further improves forecasting power and horizon. Predictability concentrates among historically more accurate, less biased managers, consistent with an information rather than a noise channel. Managerial expectations thus offer incremental insights into economic activity, with implications for macro- and microeconomic decision-making.

papers.title: The Smart Buildings Control Suite: A Diverse Open Source Benchmark to Evaluate and Scale HVAC Control Policies for Sustainability
papers.abstract: Commercial buildings account for 17\% of U.S. carbon emissions, with roughly half of that from Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC). HVAC devices form a complex thermodynamic system, and while model predictive control and reinforcement learning have been used to optimize control policies, scaling to thousands of buildings remains a significant unsolved challenge. Most current approaches are over-optimized for specific buildings and rely on proprietary data or hard-to-configure simulators. We present the Smart Buildings Control Suite, the first open source interactive HVAC control benchmark with a focus on solutions that generalize across building. It has 3 components: real-world data from 11 buildings over 6 years, a lightweight data-driven simulator, and a modular Physically Informed Neural Network (PINN) building model. The buildings span multiple climates, management systems, and sizes, and both the simulator and PINN easily transfer to new buildings, ensuring solutions using this benchmark are robust to these factors and only reliant on fully scalable building models. This represents a major step towards scaling HVAC optimization from the lab to buildings everywhere. To facilitate use, our benchmark is compatible with the Gym standard, and our data is available at our webpage. Code at https://github.com/google/sbsim

papers.title: Sample-Efficient Quantum State Tomography for Structured Quantum States in One Dimension
papers.abstract: In this paper, we answer this fundamental question affirmatively by using a class of informationally complete positive operator-valued measures (IC-POVMs), including symmetric IC-POVMs (SIC-POVMs) and spherical $t$-designs, focusing on sample complexity while not accounting for the implementation complexity of the measurement settings. For SIC-POVMs and spherical 2-designs, we show that the number of state copies to guarantee bounded recovery error of an MPO state with a constrained least-squares estimator depends on the probability distribution of the MPO under the POVM but scales only linearly with $n$ when the distribution is approximately uniform. For general spherical $t$-designs with a sufficiently large $t$, we prove that only a number of state copies proportional to the number of independent parameters in the MPO is sufficient for a guaranteed recovery of any state represented by an MPO. In addition, we establish a sample complexity lower bound based on the Cramer-Rao bound, showing that, for strictly positive definite MPO states and unbiased estimators, a number of state copies proportional to the number of independent parameters in the MPO is also necessary, although the upper and lower bounds do not yet match in their dependence on the target accuracy. Furthermore, we propose a spectral method and a projected gradient descent (PGD) algorithm to solve the constrained least-squares problem, both equipped with rigorous recovery error guarantees.

papers.title: Dual Active Learning for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
papers.abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences is critical to recent advances in generative artificial intelligence. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is widely applied to achieve this objective. A key step in RLHF is to learn the reward function from human feedback. However, human feedback is costly and time-consuming, making it essential to collect high-quality conversation data for human teachers to label. Additionally, different human teachers have different levels of expertise. It is thus critical to query the most appropriate teacher for their opinions. In this paper, we use reinforcement learning (RL) to formulate the alignment problem. Motivated by the idea of $D$-optimal design, we first propose a dual active reward learning algorithm for the simultaneous selection of conversations and teachers. Next, we apply pessimistic RL to solve the alignment problem, based on the learned reward estimator. Theoretically, we show that the reward estimator obtained through our proposed adaptive selection strategy achieves minimal generalized variance asymptotically, and prove that the sub-optimality of our pessimistic policy scales as $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ with a given sample budget $T$. Through simulations and experiments on LLMs, including annotator-level preference data and downstream Best-of-$N$ response-selection evaluations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm and its superiority over existing baselines.

papers.title: Gapped and gapless quantum spin liquids on the ruby lattice
papers.abstract: The ruby lattice has been the subject of much interest recently due to its realization in Rydberg atom arrays, where its rich variety of frustrated interactions gives rise to topologically ordered quantum spin liquids. Similarly, numerical studies of ruby-lattice spin models, with both isotropic and anisotropic interactions, have provided evidence of gapped and gapless spin-liquid ground states with different low-energy gauge structures. Motivated by these findings, we perform a projective symmetry group (PSG) classification of U(1) and $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ fermionic spinon mean-field theories$\unicode{x2014}$respecting space-group and time-reversal symmetries$\unicode{x2014}$for $S=1/2$ spins. We obtain a total of 50 U(1) and 64 $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ PSGs, and upon restricting their realization via mean-field $\textit{Ans\"atze}$ with up to second-nearest-neighbor singlet amplitudes (relevant to the models studied here), only 8 U(1) and 18 $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ distinct states are obtained. We present the singlet fields for all $\textit{Ans\"atze}$ up to third-nearest-neighboring bonds and discuss their spinon dispersions as well as their dynamical spin structure factors. Building on this information, we also obtain the phase diagram of the Heisenberg model in the presence of first- ($J_{1}$), second- ($J_{1}'$), and third- ($J_{2}$) neighbor antiferromagnetic couplings within a self-consistent mean-field approximation.

papers.title: Comparison principles for degenerate sub-elliptic equations in non-divergence form
papers.abstract: We study the comparison principle for viscosity sub- and super-solutions of degenerate quasi-linear equations in non-divergence form driven by the horizontal vector fields of a Carnot group, under an ellipticity condition and a homogeneity condition.

papers.title: Explicit expressions for iterates of power series
papers.abstract: We present several formulas for both the discrete and fractional iterates of an invertible power series $f,$ using a new unifying approach based on umbral calculus. Known formulas are extended, and their proofs simplified, while new expressions are introduced. In particular, by employing $q$-calculus identities, we eliminate the requirement for $f'(0)$ to equal $1$ and the resulting general expressions for the iterative logarithm are also obtained.

papers.title: Lower order terms in the shape of cubic fields
papers.abstract: We demonstrate equidistribution of the lattice shape of cubic fields when ordered by discriminant, giving an estimate in the Eisenstein series spectrum with a lower order main term. The analysis gives a separate discussion of the contributions of reducible and irreducible binary cubic forms, following a method of Shintani. Our work answers a question posed at the American Institute of Math by giving a precise geometric and spectral description of an evident barrier to equidistribution in the lattice shape.

papers.title: On the critical points of solutions of Robin boundary problems
papers.abstract: In this paper we prove the uniqueness of the critical point for stable solutions of the Robin problem \[ \begin{cases} -\Delta u=f(u)&\text{in }\Omega\\ u>0&\text{in }\Omega\\ \partial_\nu u+\beta u=0&\text{on }\partial\Omega, \end{cases} \] where $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ is a smooth and bounded domain with strictly positive curvature of the boundary, $f\ge0$ is a smooth function and $\beta>0$. Moreover, for $\beta$ large the result fails as soon as the domain is no more convex, even if it is very close to be: indeed, in this case it is possible to find solutions with an arbitrary large number of critical points.

papers.title: The Bruce-Roberts number of holomorphic 1-forms along complex analytic varieties
papers.abstract: We introduce the notion of the \textit{Bruce--Roberts number} for holomorphic 1-forms relative to complex analytic varieties. Our main result shows that the Bruce--Roberts number of a 1-form $\omega$ relative to a complex analytic hypersurface $X$ with an isolated singularity can be expressed in terms of the \textit{Gom\'ez-Mont--Seade--Verjovsky index} of $\omega$ along $X$, the \textit{Milnor number} of $\omega$ and the \textit{Tjurina number} of $X$. This result allows us to recover known formulas for the Bruce--Roberts number of a holomorphic function along $X$ and to establish connections between this number, the radial index, and the local Euler obstruction of $\omega$ along $X$. Moreover, we present applications to both global and local holomorphic foliations in complex dimension two.

papers.title: Some invariants of totally disconnected locally compact groups: cohomology and combinatorics
papers.abstract: The paper investigates two invariants for totally disconnected locally compact (t.d.l.c.) groups: the number of ends and the rational discrete cohomological dimension. Firstly, for a compactly generated t.d.l.c. group $G$, it is shown that its number of ends can be expressed in terms of the low-dimensional rational discrete cohomology of $G$, generalising a notable theorem by E. Specker to the t.d.l.c. setting. Secondly, we focus on a t.d.l.c. group $G$ acting under suitable conditions on a building $\Delta$, showing that both the number of ends and the rational cohomological dimension of $G$ are related to those of the Weyl group associated to $\Delta$. In special cases, we compare the rational discrete cohomological dimension of $G$ to its flat-rank, and in the appendix we provide examples for which these two invariants coincide. Finally, for t.d.l.c. groups with rational discrete cohomological dimension one that act properly and chamber-transitively on locally finite buildings, we explicitly construct a proper cocompact action on a tree out of the action on the building. All the results of independent interest in Coxeter theory have been included in the appendix.

papers.title: A phase transition for the cokernels of random band matrices over the p-adic integers
papers.abstract: Let $\mathbf{B}_n$ be an $n\times n$ Haar-uniform band matrix over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ with band width $w_n$. We prove that $\text{cok}(\mathbf{B}_n)$ has Cohen-Lenstra limiting distribution if and only if \[\lim_{n\to\infty} \left(w_n-\log_p(n)\right)=+\infty.\]

papers.title: TRAM: Test-Time Risk Adaptation with Mixture of Agents
papers.abstract: Deployed reinforcement learning agents often face safety requirements that are specified only after training: new hazard maps, revised risk thresholds, or behavioral alignment constraints. We study zero-update deployment-time adaptation in which a fixed library of risk-neutral source policies must be reused under a newly specified reward-risk tradeoff. We propose TRAM (Test-time Risk Adaptation with Mixture of Agents), a source-scored composition rule that evaluates each source under the target reward and an occupancy-based deployment risk, then selects actions using risk-adjusted source scores. Unlike training-time risk-sensitive methods tied to a fixed surrogate such as return variance, TRAM supports spatial barrier exposure, divergence to a reference behavior, and local volatility risks specified at test time. We make the surrogate nature of the method explicit: TRAM is not claimed to solve the full occupancy-control problem of the stitched policy, but it admits a measurable source-hull mismatch term connecting source-scored risk to realized risk. Experiments in gridworlds, MuJoCo Reacher, Safety-Gymnasium, and an inference-time LLM alignment setting show that TRAM improves deployment risk while preserving reward and requires no parameter updates at test time.

papers.title: A systematic framework for generating novel experimental hypotheses from language models
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) have been shown to capture complex linguistic patterns, yet their utility in understanding human language and more broadly, human cognition, remains debated. While existing work in this area often evaluates human-machine alignment, few studies attempt to translate findings from this enterprise into novel insights about humans. To this end, we propose a systematic framework for hypothesis generation that uses LMs to simulate outcomes of experiments that do not yet exist in the literature. We instantiate this framework in the context of a specific research question in child language development: dative verb acquisition and cross-structural generalization. Through this instantiation, we derive two novel, untested hypotheses: (1) the alignment between argument ordering and discourse prominence features of exposure contexts modulates how children generalize new verbs to unobserved structures; and (2) that this alignment in the first postverbal argument of the exposure context has a more noteworthy effect. Additionally, we also design a set of experiments that can test these hypotheses in the lab with children. This work contributes both a domain-general framework for systematic hypothesis generation via simulated learners and domain-specific, lab-testable hypotheses for child language acquisition research.

papers.title: Local and global existence for the stochastic Prandtl equation driven by multiplicative noises in two and three dimensions
papers.abstract: In this paper, we are concerned with the local and global existence for the stochastic Prandtl equation in two and three dimensions, which governs the velocity field inside the boundary layer that appears in the inviscid limit of the stochastic Navier-Stokes equation with non-slip boundary condition. New problem arises when establishing the well-posedness in the stochastic regime: one can never derive a pathwise control of the energy functional which is used to describe the analytic radius of the solution in the deterministic setting. To this end, we establish higher-order estimates in the conormal Sobolev spaces in order to get rid of the dependence of the analytic radius on the unknown. Three approximate schemes are constructed for solving the stochastic Prandtl equation, and a local well-posedness is obtained in a tangentially analytic and normally Sobolev-type space. Furthermore, we study the stochastic Prandtl equation driven by a tangential random diffusion, and find that the noise regularizes the equation in the sense that in both two and three dimensions, there exists a global Gevrey-2 solution with high probability and the radius growing linearly in time.

papers.title: Existence of two-dimensional deep capillary solitary water waves with constant vorticity
papers.abstract: We consider two-dimensional capillary water waves with nonzero constant vorticity in infinite depth. We first derive the Babenko equation that describes the profile of the solitary wave. When the velocity $c$ is close to a critical velocity, the Babenko equation can be reduced to the stationary focusing cubic nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation plus perturbative error. This gives the existence of small-amplitude solitary wave solutions for the water wave system with constant vorticity whose profiles are close to solutions of the stationary focusing cubic nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation.

papers.title: ProCreate, Don't Reproduce! Propulsive Energy Diffusion for Creative Generation
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose ProCreate, a simple and easy-to-implement method to improve sample diversity and creativity of diffusion-based image generative models and to prevent training data reproduction. ProCreate operates on a set of reference images and actively propels the generated image embedding away from the reference embeddings during the generation process. We propose FSCG-8 (Few-Shot Creative Generation 8), a few-shot creative generation dataset on eight different categories -- encompassing different concepts, styles, and settings -- in which ProCreate achieves the highest sample diversity and fidelity. Furthermore, we show that ProCreate is effective at preventing replicating training data in a large-scale evaluation using training text prompts. Code and FSCG-8 are available at https://github.com/Agentic-Learning-AI-Lab/procreate-diffusion-public. The project page is available at https://procreate-diffusion.github.io.

papers.title: Shockwave-Enhanced Floquet Engineering of Relativistic Quasiparticles
papers.abstract: We investigate Floquet engineering of relativistic quasiparticles driven by propagating waves, identifying distinct quantum states and phase transitions in the time-like, light-like, and space-like regimes. Using Floquet--Bloch theory, we show that the Lorentz redshift of the driving frequency in the rest frame of the wave strongly amplifies Floquet band modulation as the wave speed approaches the Fermi velocity, leading to a shockwave-like state synchronized with the wave motion. For two-dimensional Dirac fermions in an in-plane circular gauge wave, the boost also enhances the longitudinal field, so that the Floquet Dirac mass grows with the square of the Lorentz factor, and the two helicities invert the mass on opposite sides of the light line; on the honeycomb lattice this inversion is valley selective and drives a Floquet Chern transition. For three-dimensional Dirac fermions, we uncover a regime where Floquet Weyl bands emerge and transition into type-II Weyl states as the wave speed nears the Fermi velocity. These findings extend beyond electrons to quasiparticles with relativistic dispersions, with slow surface waves such as acoustic waves, plasmons, and spin waves as natural drives, opening new avenues for dynamic band engineering in quantum materials.

papers.title: Semihomogenous vector bundles, $\mathbb Q$-twisted sheaves, duality, and linear systems on abelian varieties
papers.abstract: In this paper, we point out the natural relation between $\mathbb Q$-twisted objects of the derived category of abelian varieties, cohomological rank functions, and semihomogeneous vector bundles. We apply this to two basic classes of objects, corresponding to each other via the Fourier-Mukai-Poincar\'e transform: positive twists of the ideal sheaf of one point and of the evaluation complexes of ample simple semihomogeneous vector bundles. This naturally leads to the introduction of $\mathbb Q^{\ge 0}$- graded section modules associated to line bundles on abelian varieties built by means of semihomogeneous vector bundles (containing the usual section rings). We prove a duality relation between such modules associated to dual polarizations, which is not visible at the level of the usual section rings. Other applications include formulas relating the thresholds of relevant cohomological rank functions appearing in this context. As a consequence we show a lower bound for the base point free threshold of a polarization in function of its type, and some obstructions to surjectivity of multiplication maps of global sections of certain line bundles.

papers.title: FUSE-PnPL: Flexible, Unified, Statistically Consistent, and Asymptotically Efficient Camera Pose Estimation from Points and Lines
